3  Writing in Markdown

Markdown is plain text with punctuation that describes structure rather than appearance. You identify something as a heading, quotation, citation, or code expression; the output format decides how that structure should look.

That separation is what allows the same source to become a web page, PDF, Word document, book chapter, slide deck, or tutorial.

3.1 Source versus appearance

In a word processor, “make this 18-point bold” is a visual instruction. In Markdown, ## Methods says “this is a second-level heading.” Quarto can then:

  • number it in a PDF;
  • put it in an HTML table of contents;
  • turn it into a slide boundary;
  • include it in navigation; and
  • give it an address for cross-referencing.

Semantic structure is both more reusable and more accessible than manual visual formatting.

3.2 Document metadata

A Quarto document begins with YAML metadata between --- lines:

---
title: "A reproducible analysis"
subtitle: "A synthetic training study"
author: "A. Researcher"
date: today
bibliography: bibliography.bib
format:
  html:
    toc: true
  pdf:
    number-sections: true
---

The YAML is configuration. It answers questions such as:

  • What is the document called?
  • Who wrote it?
  • Which bibliography should be used?
  • Which outputs should be created?
  • Which options differ between those outputs?

Indentation defines nesting:

format:
  html:             # belongs under format
    toc: true       # belongs under html
  pdf:              # also belongs under format
    number-sections: true

If toc were aligned with format, it would have a different scope.

3.3 Headings create document structure

Use one # for a level-one heading, two for level two, and so on:

Source

# Introduction

## Background

## Research question

# Methods

## Data

## Analysis

Rendered structure

1 Introduction
  1.1 Background
  1.2 Research question
2 Methods
  2.1 Data
  2.2 Analysis

The precise numbering and typography come from the output format.

Do not skip from # to ### simply because you prefer the smaller font. That creates a broken outline for navigation and assistive technology. Change the theme if the visual design needs adjustment (more on this later).

3.4 Section numbering and cross-references

Turn on numbering for an output:

format:
  html:
    number-sections: true
  pdf:
    number-sections: true

Give a heading a stable identifier:

## Statistical analysis {#sec-statistical-analysis}

Refer to it with:

The model specification is described in @sec-statistical-analysis.

Quarto writes “Section 3.2” or the appropriate number. If the section moves, the reference updates automatically.

Source

## Data preparation {#sec-data-preparation}

Missing values were retained for descriptive checks.

## Statistical analysis

See @sec-data-preparation before fitting the model.

Rendered idea

3.1 Data preparation
Missing values were retained for descriptive checks.

3.2 Statistical analysis
See Section 3.1 before fitting the model.

Stable identifiers are better than writing “see the section above” or manually typing “Section 3.1”. Use short, descriptive, lowercase labels separated by hyphens.

Quarto uses the same system for sections, figures, tables, equations, listings, and exercises:

Object Label prefix Reference
Section sec- @sec-methods
Figure fig- @fig-change
Table tbl- @tbl-summary
Equation eq- @eq-change
Listing lst- @lst-model

3.5 Paragraphs and emphasis

A blank line starts a new paragraph. A single line break in the source normally continues the same paragraph, allowing you to wrap source text without changing the rendered prose.

Source

This is one paragraph even though the
source wraps across two lines.

This is a new paragraph with *emphasis*,
**strong emphasis**, and `inline code`.

Rendered

This is one paragraph even though the source wraps across two lines.

This is a new paragraph with emphasis, strong emphasis, and inline code.

Use emphasis to convey meaning, not to simulate headings. Backticks are useful for filenames, functions, variables, and short commands.

3.6 Lists

Unordered lists use -; ordered lists use 1.. Markdown can number ordered lists automatically:

Source

The analysis will:

- read the source data;
- derive the change score; and
- produce a figure.

The reader should:

1. open the project;
1. render the manuscript;
1. inspect the output.

Rendered

The analysis will:

  • read the source data;
  • derive the change score; and
  • produce a figure.

The reader should:

  1. open the project;
  2. render the manuscript;
  3. inspect the output.

Using 1. for every ordered item makes rearranging source easier. Use explicit numbers only when the source number itself matters.

3.7 Links, images, and footnotes

[Quarto documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/)

![A concise description of the image](images/result.png)

This claim needs a qualification.[^qualification]

[^qualification]: The data are synthetic and illustrate workflow only.

Good link text tells the reader where the link goes. Avoid “click here”.

Image text inside ![...] becomes alternative text. Describe the information a reader needs, not merely the filename or “image of a graph”.

Footnotes are appropriate for supplementary explanation. If information is central to interpreting the result, keep it in the main text.

3.8 Quotations and block quotes

Prefix quoted paragraphs with >:

Source

> Reproducibility is a property of a
> workflow, not simply a file format.

Rendered

Reproducibility is a property of a workflow, not simply a file format.

For published words, include a citation and page or section locator where appropriate. Markdown syntax does not remove scholarly attribution requirements.

3.9 Callouts

Callouts separate warnings, definitions, tips, or assumptions from the main narrative:

::: {.callout-warning}
The data are synthetic and must not be interpreted as evidence.
:::
Warning

The data are synthetic and must not be interpreted as evidence.

Common types are note, tip, important, warning, and caution. A callout should add meaning, not turn every paragraph into a coloured box.

3.10 Tables written in Markdown

Small, static tables can be written directly:

Source

| Format | Best suited to |
|---|---|
| HTML | Browsing and interaction |
| PDF | Fixed-page distribution |
| DOCX | Editorial workflows |

Rendered

Format Best suited to
HTML Browsing and interaction
PDF Fixed-page distribution
DOCX Editorial workflows

Use a code-generated table when values come from data. A hand-written Markdown table is appropriate for stable explanatory content such as option summaries.

3.11 Mathematics and numbered equations

Inline mathematics uses one pair of dollar signs:

The individual change is $\Delta_i = y_{i1} - y_{i0}$.

The rendered result is: the individual change is Δi=yi1−yi0\Delta_i = y_{i1} - y_{i0}.

A display equation uses $$. Add a label inside braces for numbering and cross-referencing:

$$
\bar{\Delta}_g =
\frac{1}{n_g}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\Delta_i
$$ {#eq-group-change}

Group means are defined in @eq-group-change.

Δ‾g=1ng∑i=1ngΔi(3.1) \bar{\Delta}_g = \frac{1}{n_g}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\Delta_i \qquad(3.1)

Group means are defined in Equation 3.1.

3.12 Citations and bibliographies

Bibliographic records live in bibliography.bib. A record has a citation key:

@article{knuth1984,
  author = {Knuth, Donald E.},
  title = {Literate Programming},
  year = {1984}
}

Use the key in prose:

Source

Literate programming was formalised by
@knuth1984.

Reproducibility requires more than
retaining code [@sandve2013].

Rendered

Literate programming was formalised by Knuth (1984).

Reproducibility requires more than retaining code (Sandve et al. 2013).

Quarto formats the citation and builds the reference list. A Citation Style Language (.csl) file can change the style without rewriting citations.

Useful citation patterns include:

[@knuth1984]                 # parenthetical
@knuth1984                  # textual author
[@knuth1984, pp. 100–102]   # locator
[@knuth1984; @sandve2013]   # multiple sources

The bibliography automates formatting, not source evaluation. Check names, titles, dates, identifiers, and whether the cited source supports the claim.

Probably the easiest way to get bib keys is from Zotero and the Better BibTeX extension which can export the required format for a .bib file automatically.

3.13 A fuller Markdown exercise

In manuscript.qmd:

  1. Complete the title, subtitle, author, and output options in YAML.
  2. Create Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and References sections.
  3. Add stable sec- identifiers to Methods and Results.
  4. Refer to Methods from the Results prose.
  5. Add a research question, bulleted aims, and the numbered change-score equation.
  6. Add one citation, one footnote, one link, and one warning callout.
  7. Render to HTML and inspect the table of contents, numbering, and references.
  8. Render to PDF and identify what changed visually and what remained semantically the same.

3.13.1 Checkpoint

The source contains structure rather than manual styling. Headings appear in navigation, section and equation references update automatically, and citations are generated from the bibliography.

Chapter 4 applies the same source-to-output principle to calculated values, figures, and tables.

Knuth, Donald E. 1984. “Literate Programming.” The Computer Journal 27 (2): 97–111. https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/27.2.97.
Sandve, Geir Kjetil, Anton Nekrutenko, James Taylor, and Eivind Hovig. 2013. “Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research.” PLOS Computational Biology 9 (10): e1003285. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003285.
